title.en: Changes Around Us: Physical and Chemical

text.en: Ice melts into water and can freeze again. Bread burnt into toast cannot become bread again. Some changes can be reversed and some cannot.

In a physical change no new substance is formed. Melting ice, dissolving sugar, cutting paper and stretching a rubber band are physical changes. Many physical changes can be reversed.
In a chemical change a new substance is formed with different properties. Burning wood, rusting iron, cooking food and souring milk are chemical changes. Signs include a change in colour, gas bubbles, heat or light, or a new smell. Chemical changes are usually permanent.
Rusting needs iron, air and water. We prevent it by painting, oiling or galvanising. Burning needs a fuel and oxygen. A fire is put out by removing one of these.
Crystals of salt or copper sulphate can be made by evaporating a saturated solution slowly. This is a physical change.
Some changes help us, like cooking. Some harm us, like rusting. Some are slow, like ripening, and some are quick, like burning a match.

problem.en: Is cooking an egg a physical or chemical change?

text.en: A new substance with different properties forms.
It is a chemical change and cannot be reversed.

prompt.en: How can you tell if a change is chemical?

requiredIdeas.en: Often with gas, heat, colour or smell.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking all reversible changes are physical or all irreversible changes are chemical.
